CHAPTER V
                           GIN



G     I N , the very best gin, is the pride of H o l ­
       land.    A D u t c h m a n ' s opinion of the sort
of gin we dared to consume under Prohibition
reeks of contempt.       When the fearsome stuff had
the effrontery     to masquerade under a D u t c h
label, it broke his heart.
   There are, however, authoritative experts to
insist that British gin is far superior in flavor to
D u t c h gin, and that some pretty good gin can
come out of the United States.           Still, Holland
can claim the greater fame.
   O f course that Prohibition gin wasn't really
gin at all.    It was alcohol merely flavored with
oil of glycerine and juniper berry.       T h e gin that
sets a D u t c h m a n   bragging is a compounded
spirit, prepared b y distilling pure spirit        with
juniper berries, coriander seeds, angelica seeds
and some precious secret essential oils.      G i n pro-
                            35
36             BACCHUS B E H A V E !


duced by the distilling process has a vastly more
delicate flavor, and has a more mellowing effect
on the t u m m y than any achieved b y mere m i x ­
ing. T h e best gin has an alcoholic strength of
about 36 per cent, although there are 48 per cent
brands, to be handled only b y experts.
   Ever since Charles Dickens had Sary G a m p
partaking of her thimbleful o' comfort, gin has
been regarded as a vastly better spirit for women
than whisky. In the main, women prefer gin as
being far less disastrous to the complexion.
   However, American men have taken to gin
like mice to cheese. Two-thirds of our cocktails
call for gin as the main ingredient. This does
not necessarily make them effeminate, as D u t c h ­
men will readily agree. B u t , as is usual with the
American male of the species, he seems to think
it makes the thing more masculine if he takes
ten thimblefuls at a time instead of one.
   It is this sort of thing which makes the con­
noisseur despair of him. So m u c h affectionate
pride and ritual g o into the preparation of the
best gin. It is a sacred ceremonial. Doled out
tenderly in precious thimblefuls at the right time
                           GIN                         37

in the right company, it can indeed be a boon
and a blessing to mankind.
   Dishonest gin should, of course, be completely
ostracized from polite society. Even disguised in
cocktails it's an affront, on a par with serving
methylated spirits.
   B u t honest gin,   now....   It shines at its best
served straight, in a thimble-sized glass which has
been rinsed out with orange or A n g o s t u r a bitters.
T h e ideal time for this is about twenty minutes
before partaking of a good A n g l o - S a x o n , Scandi­
navian or Teutonic meal. It is the preferred
aperitif for a meal at which beer, ale or stout are
to be served, as distinct from wine. A n d , if you
are sure of your gin, one drink is enough. In
fact, it's almost blasphemy to overdo it. T h a t is

WINES



I T is told of K i n g E d w a r d V I I that he once felt
   called upon to reprove a Foreign Ambassador
at his table.
   H e had, you see, honored the gentleman by
having a peculiarly fine French wine served at
dinner...    a revered and precious vintage of
the highest quality.
   T h e Ambassador, seated at his right, lifted his
glass and drank the wine at one gulp.
  K i n g E d w a r d gazed at him reproachfully, and
admonished:
   "Mr. Ambassador, when you meet a great
wine of France you breathe it, hold it to the
light, you touch it t o your lips, you put your
glass down and talk about it. . . . "
    A s to talking about it, we have the story of
the gourmet uncle who was entertaining his
y o u n g sprig of a nephew, just home from col-
                          50
                          WINES                           51

lege. Uncle, in his expansive hospitality, ordered
a bottle of the finest wine in his cellar. N e p h e w
partook of it without comment. Uncle began
to think this precious nectar was wasted on the
young squirt, so his next order to his butler was
for an inferior wine.
   N e p h e w seemingly drank this with relish.
   "Fine wine, sir," he said. " V e r y excellent."
    " W h y , you y o u n g j a c k a s s , " snorted Uncle.
" T h e first bottle was beyond compare, b u t this
stuff, b a h ! "
   " I k n o w , " smiled the y o u n g m a n c o m f o r t ­
ably.     " T h i s one needs recommending, the
other didn't."
  In a general way, it is safer to compliment the
host on his fine wines; he can so easily be counted
upon to have an E d w a r d V I I complex in the
matter.
   It is highly desirable to cultivate your own
taste and discrimination for wines if you would
stand well with the best hosts. A n d , ahem, to
have a host, y o u m u s t be a host.
   Y o u r duties as a host are even more impor­
tant. Y o u owe it to the honor of your country
52               BACCHUS BEHAVE!

to aid in elevating its drinking standards to the
loftiest pinnacle of social distinction.    You must
neither affront the palate of an epicurean guest,
nor pander to the low-brow tastes of an igno­
ramus.
  N o t h i n g can stir u p more emotional argument
than the subject of wines.       Infinite reverence,
prayer, time and artistry go into their proper
preparation.     Every one of the several hundred
famous wines are the products of geniuses in
their line. T h e great wine makers have the souls
of artists.    A n d , like artists in other walks of
life, they are strong in their hypercritical prefer­
ences and in their interpretations of what con­
stitutes the true and the beautiful.       Every wine
artist has his ardent disciples, so there are lots
of jolly schools of wine-thought to choose from.
  There is, however, one point upon which all
agree—the precious ritual        and respect     with
which wines must be served and enjoyed.

recipes.raw_text:
ON   B E I N G A GOOD G U E S T



A     G O O D guest will never strain that social
      rule which requires a host to exercise u n ­
swerving patience and consideration for the
visitor within his gates.
   H e will see to it that his host is charmed b y
his presence.
   T h e responsibilities of the guest extend be­
yond his own personal pleasure and behavior.
H e will not only endeavor to make himself
agreeable to every one present, b u t evince a gen­
eral satisfaction with everything provided.
   There are two kinds of guests who often try
the souls of hosts. There is the haughty, critical
epicure who manages to convey the impression
that nothing is quite satisfactory, even when his
disapproval is silent; and there is the ignorant,
self-licensed fellow who is just plain hoggish.
   Both are obnoxious. A n d their obnoxiousness
                         101
102            BACCHUS BEHAVE!

becomes even more evident where liquor is
served.
   If, when your own palate has cultivated a nice
discrimination, your host serves inferior or
erroneous liquid refreshment, just being g o o d -
temperedly abstemious will meet the situation
nicely. It is unnecessary and undesirable to
flaunt your epicurean erudition.
   Y o u m a y have to resort to strategy if the
stuff is undrinkable. There was the case of the
sensitive connoisseur who, wishing to show a
nice respect for both his hostess and his own
stomach, surreptitiously watered a healthy fern
with his cocktail. T r u e , the fern showed a
swift and painful decline—but it was sacrificed
in a good cause ... the lesser of three evils.
   Otherwise just sip the stuff—it is perfectly
good form not to drain the glass. A f t e r all, the
more cultivated palates amongst us have had
plenty of practice in this art of splendid m o d ­
eration during the recent painful era of hasty
home-brews and the stuff which the bootlegger
assured the host was " p r e - w a r . "
   B u t , at that, your critical epicurean is more
           ON   B E I N G A GOOD   GUEST         103

easily tolerated than the fellow who is content
to swill down anything that is offered and seems
to consider that copious consumption is the
be-all and end-all of the party. H e is usually
both expensive and unpleasant.
   There are three excellent reasons for moder­
ation in a guest. If the liquor is above reproach,
it should be treated with reverence and respect­
ful obeisance. It probably cost a pretty penny,
and every precious drip should be slowly, honor­
ably appreciated. It should n o t be quaffed in
vulgar haste, b u t lingered over.
   If, on the other hand, its quality is indifferent,
the guest m a y conscientiously consider his own
innards. In which case, he will likewise imbibe
slowly and meagerly, if not reverently.
   A n d again, either way, if a guest imbibes with
too m u c h enthusiasm, he not only commits the
social crime of becoming a nuisance, b u t he does
so at the expense of his host, the last atrocity.

STRANGE NECTARS

   AN important     point in the art of      correct
     drinking is to sample strange nectars with
caution.
  Imagine the embarrassment of a polite drinker,
well versed in the use of all the more widely
known liquors, when he first meets, say, okole-
hau, the famous Hawaiian drink, and imbibes it
as he would beer!
  T h e traveler finds himself confronted       with
strange nectars in m a n y ports.   Perhaps there is
no friend to guide him as to each one's class dis­
tinction.   It might come within the category of
wine, spirit, beer or grape-juice, for all he knows.
Some most distressing debacles have         resulted
from this sort of inexperience.
  For instance, the saki of J a p a n has the appear­
ance of an innocent white wine.      It is served in
small china bowls.     T h e stranger within their
                         115
 116             BACCHUS BEHAVE!

gates is tempted to partake of it with the same
unconcern with which he would quaff Sauterne
or Riesling. This is a grave error.     There are sakis
and sakis, and some of them are alarmingly potent.
It's almost the difference between a weak high­
ball and straight raw whisky.         S o , for the sake
of your national honor, approach your introduc­
tion to J a p a n ' s nectars with extreme caution.
   T h e okolehau of H a w a i i is insidious stuff, bent
on mischief.     It can do appalling things to an
unversed stomach.       J u s t as well to treat it with
the same abstemiousness one accords to liqueur
until one has become more familiar with its little
ways.
   T h e same m a y be said of the pontacq of South
Africa.   This has all the appearance of an inno­
cent red claret—which it certainly does not live
u p to on a too enthusiastic first acquaintance.
  This is likewise true of the Mexican tequila.
  In Persia they will serve you arogh, which is
remotely related to gin but thrice as strong.
  T h e v o d k a of Russia, as imbibed b y hardened
Russians, is no drink for an amateur.        It's a sort
                  STRANGE        NECTARS           117

of gangster relative of brandy, which that hon­
orable family would wish to repudiate.
   A Hollywood host received a present of a case
of bottled liquid from an Oriental friend            in
China.     T h e accompanying letter indicated that
it was a Manchurian wine of exceptional charm
which would transform the most modest meal
into a Lucullean banquet.
   A party was obviously in order.           T h e host
served the wine with the later courses in claret
glasses.    T h e result was almost instantaneously
disrupting.     Staid dowagers of unimpeachable
dignity, down to the least of the guests, behaved
with deplorable informality.          T h e butler took
c o m m a n d of the situation as well as he was able,

u r g e n t confidential call.
